newsitem.title: ALBANIA: ICRC believes one in 10 Albanians needs aid.
newsitem.headline: ICRC believes one in 10 Albanians needs aid.

text.p: The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has distributed food aid and medicines across violence-plagued Albania since last month and estimates one in 10 Albanians needs relief, a spokeswoman said on Monday.
Nina Winquist-Galbe told Reuters that the Geneva-based ICRC had distributed 40 tonnes of food and 15 tonnes of medicines in the small Balkan state since March 27.
"One in 10 Albanians needs humanitarian aid, but we have not come across a single person who is starving," she said.
She estimated that some 70,000 families, representing 10 percent of Albania's population of 3.4 million, needed relief.
The ICRC and U.N. World Food Programme were directing their aid mainly at institutions and poor families, officials said.

State food supplies were not reaching hospitals, orphanages or homes for the handicapped and elderly outside Tirana, Winquist-Galbe said. The poorest families were hardest hit by sharp increases in the prices of basic foodstuffs.
The ICRC estimated that there were an estimated 6,000-7,000 patients in hospitals and 750-1,000 children in orphanages in Albania, the spokeswoman said.
Albania crumbled into near-anarchy after the collapse in February of fraudulent savings schemes in which many had invested their life savings.
A U.N.-approved multinational security mission, which will eventually total 6,000 troops from eight countries, will deploy in force on Tuesday to protect distribution of the aid.
Unlike the WFP, the ICRC's policy is not to accept armed escorts while distributing aid, Winquist-Galbe said.
"The ICRC believes that humanitarian work must be disassociated from military operations," she said.
Earlier, the WFP, the world's largest international food aid organisation, said it would rely on the multinational mission to escort it in unsafe areas.
"We will not distribute food unescorted to places that are not secure," spokeswoman Laura Boldrini told Reuters.

The ICRC plans its distributions of aid meticulously in order to reduce risks, by checking routes, seeking the advice of hospital authorities and local Red Cross offices as far as possible, Winquist-Galbe said.
She said the ICRC distributed small quantities of aid -- one or two weeks' supply of food -- at a time to institutions in order not to put them at risk from looting.
Gunmen shot and wounded two doctors at a hospital in rural Albania over the weekend, state television showed. The motive for that attack was unclear.

The ICRC's food aid, mainly rations of pasta, rice, oil and beans, and a wide range of medicines and surgical supplies had been delivered to Albania by land from a warehouse in Ionnina in northern Greece, Winquist-Galbe said.
She said the ICRC planned to distribute 11.5 tonnes of food aid in Albania this week.
